name: Okra
summary: A frost-sensitive warm-season vegetable grown for its tender immature pods. Harvesting every few days helps prevent pods becoming tough and fibrous; cultivar-specific size, pod color and spinelessness are not assigned to this species-level entry.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Abelmoschus esculentus in Malvaceae. UF/IFAS documents several distinct okra cultivars, but this identity does not represent any one of them.

cultivation.short: Full sun, warm weather and well-drained soil
cultivation.guidance: UGA Cooperative Extension recommends full sun and well-drained soil for home-garden okra; it notes moisture matters during flowering and pod development. In its Georgia guidance, deep watering may be needed during extended dry periods. UF/IFAS distinguishes lighter, more frequent irrigation for establishing seedlings from deeper irrigation for mature field plants. These regional soil-garden recommendations are not container or hydroponic prescriptions. Avoid persistently wet soil and overapplying nitrogen: UF/IFAS reports excessive leafy growth can reduce pod production.

care.short: Use a soil test; excess nitrogen can favor leaves over pods
care.guidance: UGA Extension advises testing garden soil and following the resulting local recommendations; it warns that overusing nitrogen can cause excessive vegetative growth with poor yield. Its example fertilizer rates are Georgia home-garden guidance and are not copied here as a universal dose. UF/IFAS likewise warns that high nitrogen can favor leaves over pods in its South Florida production context.

growth.short: Upright pod-bearing plants; final spacing varies by cultivar
growth.guidance: Okra is grown for its edible pods. UGA advises thinning home-garden plants to about 1.5–2 feet apart after establishment, while UF/IFAS notes spacing varies with variety and branching habit. Treat this as outdoor soil-bed guidance only—not indoor pod spacing. Cultivar-independent mature dimensions and container fit are not established for this identity.

harvest.guidance: Harvest immature pods while tender, commonly around 2–3 inches in UGA and UF/IFAS guidance; timing and acceptable size vary by cultivar. UGA reports harvest beginning roughly 60–70 days after planting in its regional home-garden guidance, while UF/IFAS recommends checking every two to three days in South Florida. Frequent picking prevents overmature, fibrous pods and supports continued production. Handle carefully: plant and pod spines can irritate skin, and branches are brittle.

problems.short: Watch for sap-feeding pests and wet-soil/root problems
problems.guidance: UF/IFAS reports aphids, thrips, leaf beetles and whiteflies as South Florida okra pests, along with root-rot and nematode concerns. This is a regional crop-risk list, not a diagnosis. These species-level sources do not establish cultivar-specific disease resistance or a universal home treatment; seek local Extension identification if damage is significant.

name: Vegetable Amaranth
summary: A warm-season leafy vegetable distinct from grain amaranths and ornamental cultivars. This entry does not imply a named color or cultivar selection.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Amaranthus tricolor in Amaranthaceae. UF/IFAS specifically treats this species as vegetable amaranth and distinguishes leafy vegetable types from grain and ornamental amaranths; no cultivar is specified.

cultivation.short: Warm-season leafy crop; maintain even moisture
cultivation.guidance: UF/IFAS describes full-sun preference with partial shade tolerated in hot conditions, and regular even irrigation. Severe water deficit can trigger early flowering and reduce yield; standing water may contribute to root rot. Recommendations are from a Florida vegetable-crop guide, not an indoor hydroponic protocol.

care.short: No amaranth-specific fertilizer dose is established
care.guidance: UF/IFAS says no fertilizer recommendation is available for vegetable-amaranth growers in Florida and mentions leaf-lettuce field rates only as a temporary stand-in for commercial growers. It also warns that excessive inorganic nitrogen may pale foliage and promote nitrate accumulation. Those field rates are not an amaranth-specific home-container or hydroponic dose, so this profile does not provide a fertilizer quantity.

growth.short: Upright leafy growth; support may be needed in some conditions
growth.guidance: UF/IFAS reports that vegetable amaranth can grow tall and may need support, but size depends on conditions and selection. The crop guide recommends thinning garden-grown plants as they grow; its field row distances are not indoor pod spacing.

harvest.short: Partial-leaf cuts can support a follow-up harvest
harvest.guidance: For repeated harvest, UF/IFAS recommends removing part of a leaf first, allowing the plant to regrow, and harvesting again over the following two weeks. It reports that leaves become fewer and unsuitable for harvest once flowering begins. These are crop-guide observations for Florida, not a guaranteed schedule for every selection or indoor system.

problems.short: Avoid severe drought and waterlogged roots
problems.guidance: UF/IFAS associates severe water deficiency with early flowering and lower yield, and excessive standing water with root-rot risk. Its regional guidance does not establish cultivar-specific disease resistance.

name: Prayer Plant
variety: Species-level houseplant identity; no named cultivar represented
summary: A tropical foliage houseplant with patterned leaves that change position between day and night. This species-level record does not select among named cultivars.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Maranta leuconeura in Marantaceae and lists several former names as synonyms. NC State documents commonly cultivated forms; no cultivar is assigned to this identity.

cultivation.short: Bright indirect light, humidity, and evenly moist growing-season soil
cultivation.guidance: NC State recommends bright indirect light, high humidity, and evenly moist potting soil during active growth, with reduced watering in winter. Too much direct sun can bleach foliage. This is container-houseplant guidance and not a hydroponic specification.

growth.short: Low, spreading foliage; rolled new leaves unfold and mature leaves move at night
growth.guidance: NC State describes horizontal spread, variegated ovate leaves, and new leaves emerging as rolled tubes; mature leaves move from a daytime horizontal position to a more upright position at night. The source gives broad dimensions across houseplant settings; no single mature size or cultivar color pattern is assigned here.

flowering.short: Small, inconspicuous flowers are rare indoors
flowering.guidance: NC State says this species can bloom under ideal conditions, but the flowers are small and insignificant and rarely appear indoors; the plant is primarily grown for patterned foliage. Its page describes colors across cultivated forms, so this species-level record assigns no flower color.

propagation.guidance: NC State recommends propagation by rhizomatous division. That is the documented practical route represented here; the source does not provide a seed-starting protocol for this houseplant.

problems.short: Low humidity, direct sun, cold drafts, and waterlogged soil can cause problems
problems.guidance: NC State notes intolerance of direct sunlight, low humidity, low temperatures and cold drafts, potential leaf burn from fluoride or excess fertilizer, and root-rot risk in poorly drained soil. It also reports that leaves may lose color under low light or low fertility; that change is a cue to review both conditions, not a diagnosis. The source reports no serious pest or disease problems, while noting occasional spider mites or mealybugs.
